p: Front Range Orbital has won the biggest job it's ever had: HEARTH, a habitat module for Halo Orbital's station, built for a crew of four and due to launch in thirty months.
In her first week Nadia asked Halo to define the contract's ninety cubic meters, and the answer came back in writing: space a crew can actually use.
Odette from FRO's small safety office asked where the crew goes if the air goes bad, and nobody had an answer.
Helen Cho-Ramirez at Halo said what she really needs: if the galley catches fire at three in the morning, all four get out before the smoke gets them.
Her Monday email asks for one number before anybody draws a wall, the time from bunk to hatch.
Tiago Ferreira. Integration and test lead, and a test person like Nadia.
Helen Cho-Ramirez. Halo's crew operations director. She wants the bunk to hatch time.
Amara Osei. Program manager. She wanted to skip two reviews to save six weeks.
Wes Harland. Chief engineer. He's stopped calling Nadia test kid, mostly.
Jun Takeda. Junior engineer, now on the system model full time.
Odette. FRO's quiet safety engineer, in the work from week one.
Chapter two. What They Actually Need.
Week two came in with snow. The plows had pushed it up against the old Centennial Lighting Works sign, and by Monday afternoon somebody had drawn a space station in it with a finger.

Tiago spent that Monday on his knees in the high bay with four rolls of blue tape. When he stood up there was a rectangle on the concrete eight meters long and four point four wide, HEARTH laid out flat, with a red X at one end for the hatch. Inside it he'd taped Wes's sketch from the first week: two crew quarters near the hatch, the galley in the middle, two more quarters past it, and the hygiene station at the far end. Smallest apartment in Colorado, he said. Four roommates. No balcony.

Helen Cho-Ramirez came on Wednesday. She was smaller than her voice on the phone, with reading glasses pushed up into gray hair and a carry-on she never set down. She didn't want coffee or a tour. She wanted the tape.
She stood on the red X for a long time. Then she walked the length of the module slowly, heel to toe, counting under her breath, and stopped in the square that was the galley.
Can I tell you why I'm going to be difficult about this? she said.
You haven't been difficult, Nadia said.

Give it a week. She looked down at the tape. Nine years ago I was the flight surgeon on console the night the old station's galley caught fire. A food warmer. Three in the morning their time. I had the crew loop in one ear and the cabin numbers in front of me, and for five minutes the only useful thing I could do was write down the time.
She took out her wallet and unfolded a yellow sticky note that had stopped being sticky a long time ago.
The sticky note from Helen's wallet. 3:12, alarm. 3:13, masks. 3:15, the commander says smoke in the galley. 3:17, all four at the node. 3:31, air clear.

Nobody was hurt, she said. People say that like it's the end of the story. It was five minutes. One of them had earplugs in and his door shut, and he was the last one out, and I watched that clock the whole time he wasn't answering. She folded the note along its old crease and put it back. I've carried this around for nine years. I'd like it to be the only one.
Then she straightened up. Now show me where they sleep.
Rosie had asked Nadia the same thing about the purple rocket on the fridge. Nadia still didn't have an answer. She walked Helen down the tape.
Helen had two days at FRO before her flight home. Amara had booked her into a conference room with a projector and a stack of Halo's old requirements documents.
Helen looked at the stack and then out the window at the high bay. I can read those on the plane, she said.

Nadia takes Helen and Odette out to the tape for both days, to walk a normal day and then a fire. They walk it end to end, then again with the lights in the high bay turned down. Helen keeps stopping to say things she'd never have said in a conference room: the crew sleeps with their heads toward the hatch, they keep shoes clipped by the bunk, nobody can find a mask in the dark. Jun fills four pages.
Elicitation draws needs out of people. Walking real scenarios in a mockup, with the stakeholder and the specialists together, brings out needs an interview list would never reach.

Thursday Amara caught Nadia at the coffee machine. Helen's great. I love Helen. But I've got a requirements review on the calendar and Halo's crew office is about to own two of your weeks. How long does this take, and what do I get at the end?

Nadia writes Amara a plan for the needs work, tied to the review date, and it fits on one page. Elicitation sessions with dates, Halo's people named, the scenario set, the stakeholder requirements, and the validation criteria, all due the week before the review. Amara adds it to the engineering plan, the SEMP, and to the schedule the same afternoon. Now Halo's two weeks are on my calendar too.

Project planning covers the technical work, not just the schedule. You named the activities, the people and resources, the outputs, and how you'll know you're done, and tied it all to the review it feeds.
Wes wanted the problem statement on one line at the top of every HEARTH document, and he had his own draft.
Deliver a ninety cubic meter habitat module for a crew of four, per the contract. Done. That's the problem.

She writes it around the crew: four people who have to live in there for six months and get out of a fire or a leak. Wes reads it. No volume in it. Nadia says the volume is a constraint, and it goes in the constraints list right under the sentence. He frowns at it and leaves it.

A problem statement describes the need and what success looks like, in the stakeholder's terms, without a solution. Constraints like volume are listed separately so they bound the answer without replacing the question.

Jun had a context diagram up on the big screen. HEARTH was a box in the middle. Halo Station was a box off to one side with a power line drawn to it. There was no box for the crew and none for the ground.
The crew aren't hardware, he said. And ground control is Halo's. We don't build either one. Should they even be on here?

Nadia has him draw the crew and ground control as actors, outside HEARTH's line but on the page. Jun adds two boxes and eleven lines. The crew box ends up with more lines into HEARTH than the station does. Huh, he says, and doesn't say anything else for a while.
Systems thinking starts with a deliberate boundary. HEARTH stays the thing FRO owns, and everything it depends on or affects goes in the context, so the analysis looks at the whole.
By Friday of week two Nadia had a folder of notes from Helen's two days, a stakeholder list that kept growing, and Helen's sticky note photographed on her phone.
Wes came by with Halo's old requirements in a binder clip. You've got plenty. Start writing shall statements. We'll figure out how the crew lives in it once there's something to live in.

Nadia holds off on the shall statements and writes the operations concept first, starting with a day in the life. It takes a week. The day in the life alone turns up nine needs that weren't in anybody's notes, including where four people eat at once in a galley built for two.

The operational concept describes how the system will be used, normal and off nominal, through scenarios. Writing it first means the requirements describe a system that works across a whole day, including its worst one.
Jun wanted to put the scenarios in the model. He'd sketched the fire scenario as a SysML activity diagram, with a lane each for the crew, HEARTH, the station and the ground.
Wes looked at it over his glasses. Halo's going to read a document. Write a document.

Nadia keeps the scenarios in Jun's model, and the document Halo reads comes out of it. Jun puts timing on every step and links each one to the need it serves. When Helen changes one step, the change shows up in both places, and the needs it touches light up.
Modeling the operational concept makes the scenarios traceable, consistent, and analyzable. Timing on the steps means you can run them later instead of arguing about them.

On Saturday Colleen asked Nadia to meet her at Centennial Airport. Colleen was preflighting a borrowed single engine airplane in a wind that made Nadia's eyes water. Nadia told her about the tape, and Helen standing in the galley, and the sticky note.
Good, Colleen said, running her hand along the leading edge of the wing. Now you have a stakeholder. Most programs only have a customer.
Nobody ever told me what they needed from a display, Colleen said. They told me what they hated about the old one. You had to watch them fly.

Colleen climbed in and pulled a laminated card from the side pocket. Engine fire in flight, she read off the top. Somebody sat in a chair on a quiet afternoon and imagined my worst day, step by step, so I wouldn't have to invent it at three thousand feet.
No airplane has a landing distance, Colleen said, stepping down off the wing. The airplane, the runway, the wind, and me on a bad day have one.

The fire scenario was the hard one. Jun had numbered the quarters along the tape. One and two faced each other by the hatch. Three and four faced each other past the galley, the same walk on paper. Four's opening sat half behind the hygiene station's wall, the last bunk in the module. Tiago had started calling it the far quarter, and by Tuesday everyone did. Each quarter got a curtain instead of a door. It was one of the first things Helen asked for, and nobody argued.

Jun's first draft started with a galley fire and walked through the fire: detection, alarm, suppression. Helen read it on a video call from Halo and was quiet a moment. You've written it for the fire, she said. Write it for the people.
Odette, FRO's safety engineer, had been on the call the whole time without a word. Put it in seconds, she said at the end. People hide in minutes.

They write it four times, once from each quarter. One and two are short. Three and four both have to go through the galley. Four, the far quarter, starts behind a wall and ends at the back of the line, with the fire between the bunk and the hatch. Helen reads all four and says, There. That's the scenario.

Emergency scenarios are about how people and the system respond together. Writing one from each crew position surfaces needs a single fire centered view hides: who's farthest, who passes the hazard, and how long each one takes.

Wednesday of week three Wes went down the scenario line by line in the high bay, defending his layout. Hatch opens in four seconds. The galley has an extinguisher. Every quarter meets its volume. Aisle's wider than the old station's. Show me the part that fails.
He was right. Every part passed. Nadia felt how much she wanted that to be the end of it.

Nadia doesn't argue the parts. She asks Wes to walk the fire with her from quarter four. They stand in the far quarter. To reach the hatch, the crew member in it walks toward the galley, through the galley, and past it. Wes looks down the tape and doesn't answer right away. No single part did that, he says. The layout did.

Systems thinking looks at the whole: the parts, how they interact, and the environment. The far quarter problem comes from layout, smoke, and crew together. No part fails on its own, which is why reviewing parts can't find it.
Amara wanted measures for the requirements review. Halo's going to ask how we know HEARTH is a success. I'd like to say ninety cubic meters, delivered, on schedule. That's what's in the contract.

Nadia takes the question to Helen, and they settle on five measures of effectiveness, MOEs, in Halo's own terms. The first one reads like her sticky note: all four crew at a safe location within the time each emergency scenario allows. Amara reads it and stops. Halo will sign that.

MOEs say how well the system achieves the mission from the stakeholder's view, without naming a solution. They start in mission analysis and get sharpened with the stakeholders, and later they're what validation checks.
Helen's need sat at the top of the needs list in her own words: if there's a fire at three in the morning, all four get out or to a safe place before the smoke gets them.
Nadia had to turn it into a stakeholder requirement by Friday. Jun had four drafts on the screen.

Nadia picks the draft that names no design: from any bunk, each crew member shall reach a safe location within the scenario time. Jun links it to Helen's need, the four fire scenarios and the first MOE. The time stays marked as to be determined, with the rationale noted: the old station's five minutes is the starting point, not the answer.

A stakeholder requirement turns the need into a checkable, solution independent statement with conditions and a measure, traced to where it came from. "To be determined" with a reason is honest. A design hidden in the requirement isn't.
Tiago found her at the edge of the tape on Monday of week four, still in his coat. So. Helen's going to ask how we prove it. What do we show her?

They write validation criteria for each emergency scenario: who runs it, in what conditions, and what counts as success, tied to the MOEs. The first runs can happen on the tape in a month. Tiago circles the last line. In the flight module. With crew. Lights out.

Validation shows the system meets the stakeholders' needs in its intended use. Building the criteria from the scenarios and MOEs now, and planning early and late runs, points the whole program at the right question.

They wanted a first timed walk on the tape before Jun built the depressurization scenario, to check the numbers in the model. Amara offered volunteers. I've got six engineers who'd love to leave their desks for an afternoon.

Nadia thanks Amara and asks Helen for people who've never seen the layout. Helen sends three trainers. Each one starts flat on a taped bunk, lights out, with an alarm on a speaker. The slowest one takes a wrong turn at the galley. Jun writes down every time to the second.

Validation evidence should come from representative users in conditions close to the intended use. People who don't know the layout, starting from where they'd really be, give numbers the model can trust.

Jun ran the depressurization scenario on Thursday night of week four, in the high bay, with his laptop on a folding table at the edge of the tape. Halo's reference leak. Alarm at zero. The target was all four through the hatch and the hatch closed by one hundred and twenty seconds. Jun had typed in the times from the tape, to the second.
Jun's first model run of scenario E2. Quarter four was through at 113 seconds, and the hatch closed at 133. Not met, 13 seconds over.
Nobody said anything. Quarter four's bar, with the hatch time stacked on the end of it, ran past the red line on Jun's screen. It was a short way past, which somehow made it worse.
They'd come close to writing shall statements in week two. Not one of them would have had a number for the walk from quarter four. The scenario put one there.

Wes was the one who walked down the tape first. He stood in the far quarter with his hands in his pockets and looked at the red X eight meters away. Brooks, he said, not turning around. Good thing we didn't draw walls.

Nadia walked to quarter four and lay down on the cold concrete inside the tape, head toward the hatch, the way Helen said the crew slept. From the floor the red X looked a lot farther than eight meters.
She called Helen from there. It was late in Halo's time zone and Helen picked up anyway.
We timed it, Nadia said. Depressurization. A hundred and thirty three seconds. The scenario allows a hundred and twenty.
There was a pause on the line, long enough that Nadia could hear Helen breathing.
Three and four. Four's the last one out.
Okay, Helen said, and Nadia heard a wallet open on the other end. Now we know. Write it down exactly like you just said it to me.
